why: Out-of-warranty inner-screen damage on Apple's foldable costs $999, and iFixit documents early units cracking during setup, so the repair economics and failure mode are decided now, not later.
notes: Pricing (iFixit-reported): inner-display replacement $999 out of warranty; cover-layer-only service $49, or $19 with AppleCare. The nano-texture lives on a replaceable flexible polymer cover, so the outer layer can be swapped without sacrificing the OLED beneath (unlike the original Galaxy Fold, which reviewers killed by peeling a layer).

Crease-hiding optics: some RGB subpixels are oval with varying orientations. An Apple patent application on reducing diffraction artifacts describes dividing the display into regions where subpixels have 'at least 32 unique displacements,' a geometric dithering that keeps reflection artifacts from reinforcing along the fold.

Hinge: linked metal joints (compared to a watchband) ride curved guides so pivot points act as if inside the display, reduce stretch/squeeze; synchronization gears keep joints moving together, versus the spring-loaded cams Google uses in the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. More than ten ultrathin layers glide as the screen folds; a single accordion-pleated flex cable carries video, audio, and charging since only one side has charging infrastructure.

Failure analysis is iFixit's hypothesis, not confirmed: owners report a noise then a line down the fold and a bright line across the display, some within six hours or before finishing setup. From a 3D model (teardown footage, patents, CT scans), breaks cluster near the transition from the flex-cable gap to the central hinge support; their closing simulation shows the center support bar not dropping far enough, creating a stress hotspot. Apple is replacing affected units for now.

Repairability: provisional 5/10, highest iFixit has given a foldable. Pluses: outer screen and trim come off intact, electrically releasable battery adhesive on both cells (two strips each) with metal shells reducing puncture/fire risk, flat disassembly tree, single-layer logic board. Minuses: $999 inner display, finicky adhesive fixtures, pentalobe and five screwdriver types; hinge still ingests fluorescent-powder 'dust' and crunches. iFixit still recommends a conventional phone (Fairphone 10/10) for repairability-first buyers.

Cameras: 48 MP f/1.6 main, 48 MP f/2.2 ultrawide, 12 MP f/2.2 outer selfie, plus an under-display inner selfie camera peeking through pixel-pattern gaps (same trick as the iPhone 18 Pro IR camera) that reviewers call muddy.
summary: iFixit tore down Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and gave it a provisional 5/10 for repairability, the highest it has awarded a foldable. The teardown documents how Apple hides the crease: a matte nano-texture on a replaceable flexible polymer cover scatters reflections, and irregularly oval, rotated subpixels (per an Apple diffraction-artifact patent citing 'at least 32 unique displacements' per region) act as geometric dithering. The hinge uses linked metal joints on curved guides with synchronization gears and springs, a waterdrop-style bend evolved from the 2020 Motorola Razr, and more than ten gliding layers. iFixit praises electrically releasable battery adhesive, intact trim and outer-screen removal, and a flat disassembly tree, but flags a $999 out-of-warranty inner-display repair (cover layer alone is $49, or $19 with AppleCare) and a hinge that still ingests dust. Addressing owner reports of cracks and bright lines appearing during setup, iFixit's 3D model and closing simulation suggest the failures cluster near the transition from the flex-cable gap to the central hinge support, where the center support bar may not drop far enough, though this remains a hypothesis and Apple is replacing affected units.
novelty: iFixit teardown reveals crease-hiding tricks in Apple's first foldable
audience: hardware engineers and repair/right-to-repair enthusiasts

title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
why: If you build computer-use agents, this argues the screenshot-plus-mouse default wastes round trips, and shows an agent that lets the model pick code, accessibility tree, or GUI per step posting the top OSWorld 2.0 scores among the systems compared.
notes: Hybrid Computer Use (HCU) exposes three interaction channels to the model: programmatic (code and command-line tools), semantic (accessibility tree, AX), and visual (GUI screenshots), and lets the model choose and combine them per task.
The AX tooling returns compact observations, executes actions in batches, and reports effects as AX diffs, cutting the number of model round trips versus repeated screen interpretation.
The interface guards against stale-state actions when an agent switches channels, and ships a supplementary HCU 'skill' that guides channel selection and coordination.
On OSWorld 2.0, HCU reports the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems; exact numbers, the baselines, and the specific models are not given in the abstract.
Trajectory analysis claims every evaluated model improved with HCU and beat baselines on efficiency and success, but different models distributed work across the channels differently.
Self-reported results from an arXiv cs.HC/cs.CL preprint; no methodology, ablations, or code/data links appear in the provided text.
summary: Hybrid Computer Use (HCU) is a unified interface for computer-use agents that combines three channels: programmatic interaction via code and CLI tools, semantic interaction via the accessibility tree (AX), and visual interaction via the GUI. The authors argue that screenshot-and-mouse interfaces impose a human-interaction prior and leave the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underused, so they let the model select and combine channels instead. The AX tools return compact observations, batch actions, and report effects as AX diffs to reduce round trips, and the system guards against stale-state actions when switching channels. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU is reported to achieve the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Trajectory analysis finds all evaluated models improve in efficiency and task success over baselines while allocating work across channels differently. The abstract omits concrete scores, named baselines, the models tested, and methodology.
novelty: unifies code, accessibility-tree, and GUI channels for computer-use agents
audience: agent/tooling engineers building computer-use automation

title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
why: The best of 13 model configurations fully resolves only 14 of 95 tasks when it has to discover unstated constraints, giving a concrete ceiling on how far today's agents get on messy customer delivery versus clean tickets.
notes: FDE-Gym has 95 end-to-end delivery tasks drawn from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real delivery projects; agents work in simulated environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable production-like systems.
Scoring is normalized 0 (unchanged system) to 1 (reference solution) by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, with penalties for stakeholder messages, trial runs, and waiting time.

Across 13 model configurations from seven providers, the best configuration scores a mean of 0.56 in the realistic setting and counts as fully resolving only 14 of 95 tasks (score at least 0.8 with no incident).
Discovering unstated constraints is named the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover constraints without explicit guidance.
Information discovery is not the whole gap: on the 23 tasks where the best config extracts every key fact from stakeholders, it still reaches 0.8+ business uplift on only 10.
An online platform lets humans practice forward-deployed-engineer skills under the same grading criteria; provider identities and the specific best model are not named in the abstract.
summary: FDE-Gym is a benchmark of 95 end-to-end customer delivery tasks from 20 scenarios across 18 sectors, built to test agents on the forward-deployed-engineer workflow: clarifying ambiguous requirements, working in live systems, and uncovering unstated constraints rather than executing well-specified tickets. Agents operate in simulated environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable production-like systems, and deliveries are scored by normalized improvement to the customer's own success metric (0 for unchanged, 1 for the reference solution), penalized for stakeholder messages, trial runs, and waiting time. Evaluating 13 model configurations from seven providers, the best configuration scores a mean of 0.56 in the realistic setting and fully resolves only 14 of 95 tasks (at least 0.8 with no incident). The authors identify discovering unstated constraints as the main bottleneck, but note that information alone is insufficient: on 23 tasks where the best config obtains every key fact, it reaches 0.8+ uplift on only 10. The paper also ships an online platform for humans to practice under the same grading. Provider names, the identity of the best configuration, and detailed methodology are not given in the abstract.
novelty: benchmark for ambiguous, stakeholder-driven real-world delivery tasks, not clean tickets
audience: AI agent researchers and engineers building customer-facing deployment agents

title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
why: Anthropic's steering tooling now doubles as an experimental probe: injecting a concept vector and asking the model to flag it before any output leaks gives a controlled, cue-free test of whether a model can read its own activations, with a reported 20% hit rate and zero control-group false positives.
notes: Jack Lindsey (Anthropic, 2025) injected activation patterns for concepts like denim, secrecy, or vegetables into half of many identical Claude copies, then asked 'Do you detect an injected thought?' first, so the model could not infer the answer from odd text it later generated.

On the most recent, most powerful Claude, models correctly flagged and named the injected concept in 20% of trials; control-group copies never reported an injection, which Lindsey treats as evidence the hits were not lucky guesses.

The steering builds on the May 2024 'Golden Gate Claude' demo, where dialing up one concept pattern made Claude inject the bridge into unrelated answers (claiming the bridge holds '1.6 million calories worth of steel cables').

Lederman and Mahowald (UT Austin) replicated on open-source models and split the two questions: they could degrade concept-naming without hurting detection, and failed namings often returned 'apple', suggesting the vivid descriptions are a steering artifact, not introspection.

What survived their controls is weaker 'anomaly detection': models notice something is off internally without naming it; Lindsey's Anthropic follow-up reached a similar conclusion, and MIT's Jacob Andreas says no fully 'deflationary' explanation has been pinned down yet.

Lindsey disclaimed any consciousness or subjective-experience claim; a spring 2026 paper by Ravfogel, Singh, and Linzen (NYU) argues that since nearly everything inside an LLM is internal-state processing, calling detection 'introspection' risks making the term meaningless.
summary: Quanta reports on a line of research testing whether large language models can introspect, centered on a 2025 experiment by Anthropic's Jack Lindsey. Using the activation-steering technique behind the 2024 Golden Gate Claude demo, Lindsey injected concept patterns into half of many identical Claude copies and asked each whether it detected an injected thought before any output could leak cues; the strongest Claude flagged and named the concept in 20% of trials while control copies produced no false positives. Replication by Harvey Lederman and Kyle Mahowald (UT Austin) separated detection from naming, showing that concept-naming could be degraded independently and that wrong guesses often defaulted to 'apple', which points to a steering artifact rather than introspection. What resisted their controls is a narrower 'anomaly detection' ability, which Lindsey's own Anthropic follow-up corroborated and which MIT's Jacob Andreas says lacks a complete deflationary explanation. Researchers including NYU's Shauli Ravfogel, plus Singh and Linzen in a spring 2026 paper, dispute whether any of this counts as introspection, arguing the first-order/second-order distinction is fuzzy and that nearly all LLM computation is internal-state processing. Lindsey explicitly made no claims about consciousness or subjective experience.
novelty: controlled "thought injection" test probes LLM introspection, replications contested
audience: ML researchers and engineers interested in interpretability and model self-awareness claims

title: Compiler bootstrapping depends on more than you might think
why: A from-source Go build that never trusts a prebuilt binary works on Linux but can silently fail on OpenBSD, because the bootstrap chain inherits the syscall and ABI conventions of each stage's build era, not of the OS you run it on.
notes: Go's compiler is written in Go, so a trust-free build starts from Go 1.4 (the last C-written toolchain), compiled with the system C compiler, then uses that to build newer releases in sequence per the 'Installing Go from source' version chart.

Each binary in the chain is frozen to the syscalls and ABIs current when its builder was released: Go 1.4 produces ~2014-era binaries, the Go 1.19 those build expect Go-1.4-era conventions, and so on up the chain.
Linux's strong backward compatibility with old binaries (decades-old binaries still run) makes this 'new old stock' chain work; the article notes x86 Linux as the case that holds.

OpenBSD does not guarantee ABI compatibility between releases and has made changes that affected Go, so the author expects older-toolchain binaries may not run on current OpenBSD, breaking from-scratch bootstrapping. Stated as the author's expectation, not a demonstrated failure.

A second dependency: toolchains that call the system linker, assembler, or C compiler rely on those programs' command-line arguments and behavior, which are often not treated as a stable long-term API.
Go has already had to patch the frozen Go 1.4 bootstrap branch to keep it building on modern systems; the article points to the Go 1.4 branch commit log as evidence.
summary: The post argues that bootstrapping a self-hosting compiler toolchain like Go's depends on more than having the source at each stage. Go can be built without trusting a prebuilt binary by starting from Go 1.4 (the last C-written version), then using each toolchain to build the next. But every binary produced is frozen to the syscall and ABI conventions of the era when its builder was released, so the chain only survives on operating systems that preserve backward compatibility with old binaries. Linux does this well, so the sequence works; OpenBSD, which does not guarantee ABI stability between releases, could break old Go-1.4-built binaries and complicate a from-scratch bootstrap (stated as the author's expectation). A second hidden dependency is on external tools (linker, assembler, C compiler) whose command-line arguments and behavior are not treated as stable APIs over time. The author notes Go has already patched the Go 1.4 bootstrap branch to keep it running on modern systems.
novelty: bootstrapping chains silently depend on OS ABI stability, not just source
audience: systems/toolchain engineers building compilers from source

title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
why: The AI capacity you provision in Europe is being built on subcontracting chains where a worker took a 400V/12,000A arc flash with no liable party, and an unreported TB case moved through company housing.
notes: At Google's Saint-Ghislain, Belgium site, an electrical tester (pseudonym Sandu) took an arc flash reported at 400 volts and 12,000 amps across his face and right side, burning 12% of his body (second-degree face/neck, third-degree shoulder and fingers) and putting him in a five-day induced coma; hospital records were seen by the Guardian. Belgium's labour inspectorate closed the case in late October finding no wrongdoing, and no company or contractor has been found liable.

The five-month Investigate Europe/Guardian investigation covered Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands, set against a stated 2,300+ datacentres across Europe (500+ in the UK) with hundreds more under construction.

Microsoft's Gavle, Sweden expansion (€3bn, 130 hectares, begun June 2024) runs through 148 firms under Collen Construction, including 28 direct subcontractors; Irish-owned subcontractor BenBau is named for housing described as 24 people per kitchen and 14 men per bathroom, plus reported vermin, broken ventilation and no winter heating.

A Romanian worker at Gavle tested positive for active TB in February 2026 per medical records; workers say BenBau made testing optional and moved another worker into the infected man's room. FOI requests to Sweden's work and public health authorities returned no reported outbreak.

More than 30 workers showed payslips indicating 50–60 hour weeks with no overtime or holiday pay; union Solidariska Byggare brokered a back-pay-and-site-access settlement with BenBau for 70 Romanian workers days before publication. Sweden's Work Environment Authority has opened 50 cases since 2021 at Microsoft-linked datacentre sites involving Irish firms.

Google, Microsoft, Dornan, BenBau and Collen all issued statements citing supplier codes, audits, safety procedures and labour-law compliance; the reporting attributes injuries, conditions and the TB case to worker accounts, medical/hospital records, payslips and FOI requests rather than independent adjudication.
summary: A joint Investigate Europe and Guardian investigation across Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands documents injuries, squalid housing, unpaid wages and exploitative practices among migrant workers building hyperscaler datacentres. Its central case is an electrical tester at Google's Saint-Ghislain, Belgium site who suffered a 400V/12,000A arc flash burning 12% of his body; Belgium's labour inspectorate closed the case finding no wrongdoing and no party has been held liable. At Microsoft's €3bn Gavle, Sweden expansion, built through 148 firms under Collen Construction, the subcontractor BenBau is reported to have housed workers in overcrowded quarters (24 per kitchen, 14 per bathroom) and mishandled a February 2026 active-TB case that FOI requests show was never reported to Swedish authorities. More than 30 workers showed payslips indicating 50–60 hour weeks with no overtime or holiday pay; a union brokered a back-pay settlement with BenBau days before publication. Sweden's Work Environment Authority has opened 50 cases since 2021 at Microsoft-linked sites involving Irish contractors. Google, Microsoft, Collen, Dornan and BenBau all cited supplier codes, audits and compliance; the findings rest on worker interviews, medical records, payslips and FOI responses.
novelty: migrant labor exploitation underpinning EU datacenter buildout
audience: readers tracking the human/infrastructure cost of AI datacenter expansion

title: I built a neural network using DOOM games
why: A working demonstration that neural network inference, down to integer attention and softmax, can be compiled into a Turing-complete game engine's physics and verified bit-exact, reframing "can it run DOOM" as DOOM running the computation.
notes: Mechanism: numbers are counts of voodoo dolls (extra player-1 starts that ride conveyors and trigger lines); activations/ReLU/clamp come from staircases a doll clears only above a step height; matrix multiply-adds accumulate as saturating int16 sector light levels; attention is dolls squeezing under ceilings lowered by other values. Runs on ViZDoom 1.3.2 (ZDoom-based) with Freedoom assets, UDMF maps and ACS scripts, headless.

MNIST: one map with 1,355 voodoo dolls and 158,550 sectors reads 784 pixels -> 64 hidden -> 45 pairwise score comparisons -> 10 win counts -> one-hot answer. The author reports the same integer network scores 97.16% on all 10,000 test digits; in DOOM, 99/100 and 966/1,000 sampled read correctly, every one exact. One read = 5,705 game tics, 76-99s headless or about 2.75 min in-window real time.

Exactness is the claim being tested: all 248 values per MNIST digit are read back from the running game and compared to a NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0) that never sees the map. Tamper controls in the test suite (187 tests, 88 on real headless DOOM) deliberately raise a weight line 5->6 and require the check to fail by +1 on exactly the affected inputs.

Transformers: a model trained on 136 DOOM level names (38 maps) generates invented names like GHEER; a 24,279-parameter 2-layer model on 11,341 names compiles to 106 maps, 56,390 dolls, 785,460 sectors and writes DEMON CANYON in 135s. Variants add softmax attention computed by dolls (log-spaced staircase exponentials), plus RMSNorm and a gated ReGLU MLP (doomnames_modern). --one-map --loop generates whole names with no Python between tokens.

Speed is explicitly not the point: one small MLP pass is 726 ms in DOOM vs 11 us in NumPy, roughly 70,000x slower. 1,000 MNIST digits across 14 DOOM games on a 16-core machine took 2 hours (5,696,000 tics, about 45 hours of real-time DOOM).

Caveats stated by the author: the marine's 'learning' is supervised imitation of a scripted aimbot with exact demon positions binned into 86 observations, not RL or learning from pixels. Engine limits include lost floor moves (two on one sector in one tic), teleport lines canceling earlier crossings, and maps wider than ~34,000 units misplacing objects. MIT-licensed; requires git/cmake/C compiler or a no-install Colab.
summary: doomformer compiles quantized integer neural networks into DOOM levels so that the game engine itself performs inference: multiply-adds become "voodoo dolls" crossing lava lines that raise sector light levels, activations become staircases, and attention becomes dolls passing under ceiling heights set by other values, all run headless in ViZDoom 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets. Every computed value is read back from the running game and checked bit-for-bit (tolerance 0) against an independent NumPy integer reference, with a test suite that includes tamper controls required to fail. Demonstrated models include an MNIST reader (1,355 dolls, 158,550 sectors, a reported 97.16% on 10,000 digits and exact on all sampled) and transformers up to 24,279 parameters that invent DOOM level names across pooled map instances, plus softmax attention, RMSNorm, and gated MLP variants computed entirely by dolls. Python's role is reduced to compiling maps, writing inputs, advancing the clock, reading results, and (for multi-map or text models) copying integers and picking letters, though some demos keep even the final choice and loop inside the level. The author is explicit that it is extremely slow (about 70,000x slower than NumPy, one digit taking 76-99s headless) and that the agent's "learning" is supervised imitation of a scripted aimbot, not reinforcement learning. The stated point is inversion: rather than running DOOM on unusual hardware, DOOM is used as the computer.
novelty: compiles neural nets into DOOM's game engine mechanics as compute substrate
audience: esoteric programming / computational substrate enthusiasts, ML tinkerers

title: Can GROUP BY still be optimized after all these years?
why: If your analytical queries end in GROUP BY ... ORDER BY agg DESC LIMIT K, most of the partition merges your engine does are wasted work; Pivot's slot trick skips them, and 63% of ClickBench queries fit that pattern.
notes: Standard high-cardinality GROUP BY: each thread hash-partitions its slice (ClickHouse uses 256 partitions per thread), then workers merge every partition. For a LIMIT 10 query over 4,096 partitions, the top 10 groups live in at most 10 partitions, so 4,086+ partitions get merged for nothing.

Naive pruning keeps a per-partition running total and skips merging if that total is below the current Kth-largest value; it only works under extreme skew. A partition of 100 items at 15 orders each sums to 1,500 and can't be pruned against a top-10 range of 1,000-1,300, even though no single group qualifies.

Slot method: give each partition a fixed number of slots, hash each group to a slot, track combined count per slot; prune the whole partition only if every slot total is below the current Kth value. Slots reuse existing partition-hash bits (first 3 bits pick 1 of 8 partitions, next 3 bits pick 1 of 8 slots) and slot count is independent of partition count.

The 100-items-at-15 case spread across 8 slots lands at ~180-195 per slot, below the 1,000 threshold, so it becomes prunable; flat distributions (all groups equal) gain nothing, and the engine should disable the optimization when it detects that.

Self-reported result on ClickBench Q16 (GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 10): 1.6x, from 35.6 ms to 22.2 ms, pruning over 70% of partitions. Vendor numbers, in-memory only; no methodology or hardware detail given.

Author frames this as probabilistic, Bloom-filter-style pruning from Pivot; they claim larger gains once MPP and spill-to-disk ship because skipped partitions also avoid shuffle and disk I/O. Not yet implemented.
summary: Pivot, an analytical database, describes an optimization for top-K GROUP BY queries (GROUP BY ... ORDER BY aggregate DESC LIMIT K) that prunes partitions before the expensive merge phase. In the standard algorithm, each thread hash-partitions and aggregates its data (ClickHouse, cited for comparison, uses 256 partitions per thread), then all partitions are merged even though only up to K partitions can contain the final answer. A naive fix tracks a per-partition total and skips merging partitions whose total falls below the current Kth-largest value, but it only triggers under extreme skew because many small groups can sum past the threshold. The improved method hashes each group into a fixed number of per-partition slots and prunes a partition only when every slot total is below the Kth value, giving finer granularity at low cost since slot count is independent of partition count and reuses existing hash bits. The authors report that 63% of ClickBench queries match this pattern and that Q16 improved 1.6x (35.6 ms to 22.2 ms) while pruning over 70% of partitions. The numbers are self-reported and in-memory; flat value distributions see no benefit and should disable the optimization, and the claimed larger wins from MPP and spill-to-disk are prospective.
novelty: slot-based partition pruning for top-K GROUP BY aggregation
audience: database/query engine engineers and analytics infra builders

title: New Android SMS of Death exploit can remotely crash unpatched phones
why: A working PoC now exists for an 8-byte text that silently crashes the cellular stack on Android 12 and 13, which never got the fix, and a 20-message burst can brick a phone into a 90-second reboot loop that only a factory reset clears.
notes: CVE-2026-58882 lives in Android's WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu: a header-length field is read as a signed 32-bit integer with no bounds check, becoming -2147483648 and throwing a NegativeArraySizeException that kills com.android.phone, the process managing cellular functions.

The attack is zero-click with no visible notification: the payload (01 06 88 80 80 80 00 BE) is sent as a data SMS to port 2948 and processed before reaching the inbox; crashing com.android.phone drops ongoing calls, including emergency calls.

Researcher Mark Blah reports Google patched it in the October 2026 updates for Android 14 through 17, but the article notes the flaw is not listed in Google's October bulletin; Android 12 and 13 did not receive the fix and stay vulnerable.

In testing, 20 malicious messages pushed phones into reboot loops; one Android 12 device rebooted into recovery roughly every 90 seconds and needed a factory reset. Carrier redelivery or re-processing stored messages causes repeated crashes.

Google's fix, 'Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu,' catches the exception and deletes the malicious messages from the SMS database to stop repeat crashes. A GitHub contributor, Sakis, found an ADB-based removal method, but it requires a computer and more technical skill.
A PoC that sends the malicious messages from another Android device has been published; it is a denial-of-service flaw, not code execution.
summary: A security researcher, Mark Blah, published a PoC for CVE-2026-58882, a zero-click denial-of-service flaw in Android's WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu. An 8-byte WAP Push message sent as a data SMS to port 2948 is processed before reaching the inbox and with no notification; an unbounded header-length value becomes the signed 32-bit integer -2147483648, triggering a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes com.android.phone and drops cellular connectivity, including active calls to emergency services. The article reports Google patched the flaw in the October 2026 updates for Android 14 through 17, though it is not listed in Google's October bulletin, and Android 12 and 13 did not receive the fix. In testing, 20 messages induced reboot loops, with one Android 12 device rebooting roughly every 90 seconds and requiring a factory reset; carrier redelivery or stored messages can cause repeated crashes. Google's fix catches the exception and deletes the offending messages from the SMS database, and a GitHub contributor named Sakis documented an ADB-based removal method that requires a computer. With a working PoC now public, users are advised to install the latest updates, availability of which depends on manufacturer and carrier.
novelty: zero-click PoC crashes phone process via 8-byte WAP push SMS
audience: security engineers and Android device maintainers

title: We can do better than line-buffered output
why: Line buffering can dominate runtime in non-interactive terminal tools; this shows how to get full-buffered throughput while still delivering lines promptly, with no threads.
notes:
glibc takes line buffering literally, splitting a single string into per-line write() calls (e.g. puts("a
b") yields separate writes for "a
" and "b
"); CPython flushes when its buffer holds a newline after appending, so one write(1,"a
b
",4) plus one write(1,"c
",2).
The fix borrows Nagle's algorithm: instead of flushing on every newline, flush when the buffer has been idle past a deadline chosen for human perception (the author suggests ~100ms).
A deadline_flush checks a monotonic clock between short stints of work; if multiple files are processed within the deadline, their names write out in one batch, no threads required.

The author's tugz unzip applies this to replace Info-ZIP unzip's per-filename printout, which the author says dominates extraction time for archives of many small files, without changing the CLI output format.

Claimed benefit: full-buffering speed with responsiveness indistinguishable to humans from flush-on-newline; the article offers code and strace examples but no benchmark numbers quantifying the speedup.
summary: Chris Wellons argues that the standard choice between full buffering and line buffering is a false one, and that line buffering is a real bottleneck for non-interactive terminal programs such as Info-ZIP unzip, where printing many filenames dominates extraction time. He shows via strace that glibc splits a single multi-line string into one write() per line, while CPython flushes whenever its buffer contains a newline. His alternative drops newline-triggered flushing in favor of a Nagle-style deadline: flush when the buffer has been idle longer than a perception-scale threshold (he suggests ~100ms), checked against a monotonic clock between short stints of work rather than via a thread. His tugz unzip uses this to batch multiple filenames into single writes when they fall within the deadline, preserving the usual output format while running faster. The post provides C struct and function examples but no benchmark figures.
novelty: deadline-based flushing replaces newline-triggered line buffering
audience: systems/C programmers writing CLI tools with terminal output

title: Ghostty 1.4.0
why: If you run Ghostty, 1.4.0 fixes ten security advisories, including a paste-protection bypass that can run a command without confirmation and tmux-control-mode output that crashes every window on 1.3.0/1.3.1, so upgrading closes real holes triggerable by displaying malicious output.
notes: Security: ten advisories fixed; several (Kitty graphics crash/allocation/file access, screen-clear memory corruption, zsh/bash integration OSC 52 clipboard hijack via crafted directory names, tmux control-mode crashes on 1.3.0/1.3.1) require only displaying malicious output; others need user interaction (paste, cmd-click, drag-drop). CVEs requested but not yet assigned by GitHub.

Kitty graphics now at 100% of the published spec, including animation and relative placements, which the maintainers claim makes Ghostty/libghostty the first non-Kitty terminal to do so; SIMD bulk parsing claimed ~16x faster image-payload parsing (64 MiB, x86_64 Linux, their benchmark).

Scrollback idle-compressed on macOS and 64-bit Linux, cutting physical (resident, not virtual) memory 70-90% for text-heavy history; default scrollback-limit raised from 10 MB to 50 MB. scrollback-limit renamed to scrollback-limit-bytes; new scrollback-limit-lines added.

Performance (self-reported): macOS pty now drained on a separate thread from parsing for 25-55% higher I/O throughput (M4 Max); VT parser 128 MB/s to 725 MB/s on ASCII (5.7x); cat of a 150 MB file dropped from 1.5s to 566ms. GTK renderer rewritten to EGL + DMABUF, triple-buffered, fixing blurry text under fractional scaling.

Breaking changes: copy-on-select defaults to none on macOS (was true), now accepts none/primary/clipboard/both, and clipboard copies only to the system clipboard. GTK now requires GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7, excluding Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. macOS 13 support retained (earlier plan to require macOS 14 dropped) but deprecated.

New ghostty +ssh CLI action wraps ssh, installs bundled terminfo on the remote (falls back to xterm-256color if tic is missing) and forwards COLORTERM/TERM_PROGRAM/TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION; unifies logic across bash, zsh, fish, elvish, Nushell. Release reflects 7 months, 172 contributors, 2,889 commits.
summary: Ghostty 1.4.0 (released October 27, 2026) is a terminal-emulator update spanning 7 months, 172 contributors, and 2,889 commits. It patches ten security advisories, several exploitable merely by rendering malicious output (Kitty graphics crashes and out-of-sandbox file access, memory corruption on screen-clear, shell-integration OSC 52 clipboard hijacking via crafted directory names, and tmux-control-mode crashes affecting 1.3.0/1.3.1); CVEs were requested but not yet assigned. It completes 100% coverage of the Kitty graphics protocol, including animation and relative placements, which the maintainers say makes Ghostty the first non-Kitty terminal to do so, with SIMD bulk parsing claimed ~16x faster on a 64 MiB benchmark. Scrollback is now transparently compressed while idle on macOS and 64-bit Linux, cutting resident memory 70-90% for text-heavy history and allowing the default limit to rise from 10 MB to 50 MB. Self-reported performance gains include 25-55% higher macOS I/O throughput from concurrent pty reads, a VT parser up to ~6x faster, and a rewritten GTK renderer on EGL/DMABUF that fixes blurry text under fractional scaling. Notable breaking changes: copy-on-select now defaults to none on macOS, GTK requires 4.18/libadwaita 1.7 (dropping Ubuntu 24.04 LTS), and a new ghostty +ssh wrapper unifies remote terminfo setup.
novelty: first terminal to fully implement Kitty graphics spec outside Kitty itself
audience: terminal/CLI power users and devtools engineers choosing a terminal emulator

title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
why: A nation-state crew weaponized reverse-proxy clones of legitimate sites to serve mobile exploits against anyone who visited, so patched-but-unpatched iPhones and Androids remain the soft spot.
notes: Sekoia attributes the campaign with 'moderate to high confidence' to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR); the Kremlin link is their assessment, not confirmed.
Mechanism: attackers registered lookalike domains (america250[.]holiday, theowo[.]club) as reverse proxies that served the real sites' content with malicious JavaScript injected into the traffic.
The injected JavaScript profiled the visiting device, then delivered platform-tailored payloads exploiting already-patched iOS and Android flaws, so only unpatched phones were at risk.
Payloads attempted to steal browser cookies, and in some cases Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.

Targets included america250.org (US 250th-anniversary group, cited as pretext for invitation-themed spear-phishing) and a London luxury hotel near the UK MoD and 10 Downing Street where Zelenskyy reportedly stayed October 14.
Sekoia says potentially hundreds of sites were impersonated, many tied to Russia's war against Ukraine.
summary: Security firm Sekoia reported a watering-hole campaign it attributes with moderate-to-high confidence to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). The attackers registered lookalike domains, including america250[.]holiday and theowo[.]club, and ran them as reverse proxies to legitimate sites (the America250 anniversary group and a London luxury hotel), serving real content with injected JavaScript. That JavaScript fingerprinted each visitor's device and delivered platform-specific payloads exploiting previously patched iOS and Android vulnerabilities, meaning unpatched phones were the exposed population. The payloads attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. Sekoia says potentially hundreds of sites were impersonated, many linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, and that the anniversary site was likely chosen to enable invitation-themed spear-phishing; the hotel sits near the UK Ministry of Defence and 10 Downing Street, where Zelenskyy reportedly stayed on October 14.
novelty: watering-hole attack spoofs legit sites via proxy domains to drop mobile exploits
audience: security researchers and mobile platform engineers tracking state-sponsored threats

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, robot demonstration data drops to roughly $0.80 per episode with no robot or operator in the loop, undercutting human teleoperation quotes of $117 (China) to $290 (North America) per hour of three-view data.
notes: Pipeline: a coding agent takes one calibration episode of the real robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation, writing the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge; the simulator supplies exact actions and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as multi-view photographic video, producing synchronized views labelled with the robot's actions.
Reported results on five real-robot tasks: policies trained only on farm data scored 93/100 successes vs 84/100 for policies trained on an equal count of teleoperated episodes.
Under distribution shift (unseen tablecloth, coloured light), farm-trained policies held 87/100 while teleoperation-trained policies fell to 46/100.

Cost claims: ~$21 of API usage plus $5 render contract once per task for adaptation, then $0.80 per additional episode for simulation, rendering, and review; one hour of three-view data averages $107 all-in.
Independent judges certify the expert controller and every rendered episode before admission to the dataset.
Numbers are self-reported from an arXiv preprint; no methodology for the judges, the video model, or the independent-judge setup is given in the abstract text.
summary: PyRUA-DataFarm proposes replacing human teleoperators with an LLM coding agent to generate robot training data. Given a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene, the agent rebuilds the task in simulation by writing the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge; the simulator provides exact actions while a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as consistent multi-view photographic video, yielding action-labelled data a policy can train on and deploy directly. On five real-robot tasks, the authors report policies trained solely on farm data matching teleoperation-trained policies (93 vs 84 successes in 100 trials), and holding up better under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light (87 vs 46). They cite costs of about $21 API plus $5 render per task once, then $0.80 per episode, with one hour of three-view data at $107 versus teleoperation quotes of $117 in China and $290 in North American labour. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. All figures are self-reported in the preprint and the abstract omits methodology details.
novelty: LLM coding agent replaces teleoperator to synthesize sim+video robot training data
audience: robotics/ML engineers working on data collection and sim-to-real transfer

title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
why: A 17GB model running on a laptop can read raw floating-point weight dumps and name the game a policy network was trained to play, so the "only frontier models can do this" framing around the weight-space paper is already wrong.
notes: The underlying paper, 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab, claims GPT-6 Astra can both interpret raw network weights (as text floats) and edit them to improve a model without training loops.

Willison replicates only the no-tools interpretation task: Qwen 3.8 27B (local, LM Studio) correctly identified Pac-Man (72% self-stated confidence), Pong (75%), and Breakout (88%) from raw weights of networks trained on 10x10 grid game variants; it failed on the more obscure Freeway, misreading it as Pac-Man.

Runs were slow and token-heavy: 46m with 43,506 reasoning tokens for Pac-Man, over an hour for Pong, 52m for Breakout; the default 8192 context failed and a longer window plus a raised timeout were required. Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter got Breakout in 9m41s / 19,493 tokens.

The paper's separate editing claim, that Astra edited 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to raise MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and triple IFEval, is reported as a vendor/author claim, not independently verified here.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating no-tool weight reading with tool-assisted editing; Sean Goedecke argued the editing example just repeats steps a human ML researcher would take.

Willison's own caveat: the reasoning traces are near-incomprehensible, and he suspects a human with pencil and paper could reach the same answer, so he rejects the framing that machines editing their own weights ends the age of source code.
summary: Simon Willison reproduces the central no-tools result from the 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' paper (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab), which claims GPT-6 Astra can read and edit raw neural-network weights supplied as text. Using Qwen 3.8 27B locally in LM Studio, he feeds the paper's prompts containing floating-point weights for small grid-game policy networks and gets correct identifications of Pac-Man, Pong, and Breakout (self-reported confidence 72-88%), with a failure on the obscurer Freeway. The task is expensive: tens of thousands of reasoning tokens and 46 minutes to over an hour per guess, plus an enlarged context window and raised timeout. Willison deliberately does not test the paper's more contested claim, that Astra edited 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights to raise MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%, which Matthew Honnibal and Sean Goedecke criticize as conflating weight-reading with ordinary tool-assisted ML work. His takeaway: the capability is real and interesting but the traces are barely interpretable, and the grander claims about machines rewriting themselves and ending source code are not justified.
novelty: local 27B model replicates weight-reading capability from frontier-model paper
audience: ML practitioners interested in interpretability and local LLM capabilities

title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
why: If the method holds up, a diffusion VLM can hit near-parity accuracy at roughly a third of decoding FLOPs with no training and no threshold tuning, just by skipping the image on most denoising steps.
notes: Visual tokens are 89-97% of DVLM input on the studied benchmarks, so re-processing the image at every denoising step dominates decode cost; pruning methods drop information and still reprocess what remains every step.

Diagnostic: comparing LLaDA-V predictions with and without the image, dropping the image changes a token's unmasking at only 22.8% of steps on average and as few as 7.9%, so the image is usually not decision-relevant.

LOWN predicts masked tokens without the image, then runs the image only when that prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned one; agreement 'certifies' the earlier prediction for reuse, and the count of certified tokens sets how many unmask that step.
Reported result: 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score retained across ten benchmarks at 35.3% of decoding FLOPs on average, with no training and no tuned threshold.

Authors claim it generalizes to other LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under KV caching; a fixed schedule is argued insufficient because image need varies by benchmark.
Caveats: results are self-reported and confined to LLaDA-based diffusion VLMs; the arXiv ID (2610.36671) and datestamp are anomalous, so treat provenance with care.
summary: LOWN is a training-free decoding method for diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) that decides, at each denoising step, whether to process the image at all. The authors observe that visual tokens make up 89-97% of DVLM input yet, for LLaDA-V, removing the image changes which token gets unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average (as low as 7.9%), meaning most decode compute reprocesses an image that does not affect the output. LOWN predicts masked tokens without the image and only invokes the image-conditioned forward pass when the two predictions disagree; agreement certifies the prior prediction for reuse and determines how many tokens unmask that step. The authors report retaining 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score over ten benchmarks at 35.3% of decoding FLOPs on average, with no threshold tuning, arguing an adaptive decision beats a fixed schedule because image need varies by benchmark. They further claim the approach generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs and composes with visual token pruning and key-value caching. All figures are self-reported and limited to LLaDA-family models.
novelty: certificate-based adaptive image-reuse cuts diffusion VLM decoding compute
audience: ML researchers/engineers optimizing diffusion-based multimodal model inference

title: CVE-2026-98432: Linux TCP Use-After-Free Risk and Patch Validation
why: Any internet-facing Linux host running an unpatched kernel is remotely reachable through this bug, and Anthropic's lab chain turned it into unauthenticated root in roughly 53 minutes against an MPTCP listener, including Go services that enable MPTCP by default.
notes: The defect is a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake path: tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers the request socket's ireq_opt pointer to the child socket's inet_opt without copying, while a retransmitted SYN on another CPU keeps reading that options object inside an RCU read-side critical section.

Root cause is a lifetime mismatch, readers use RCU but destructors called plain kfree(), which returns memory to the allocator before readers finish. The upstream fix, commit e3f33b0a1d89 ('ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period'), switches inet_sock_destruct() and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() to kfree_rcu().

A related request-migration variant triggers when net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program clones a request socket, leaving two objects sharing one options allocation.

The Linux CNA assigned CVSS 3.1 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H); Ubuntu also publishes a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.3 with attack requirements present and labels it high priority. The scores characterize the upstream component, not any specific vendor build.

Anthropic's October 27 post claims a zero-click PoC against an MPTCP listener that leaked a kernel pointer to defeat KASLR in ~48 minutes, then reached root command execution in another ~5 minutes; failed attempts leave the handshake incomplete without crashing, allowing retries. The article stresses this is one lab configuration, not measured prevalence or a universal success rate.

Go services can expose MPTCP listeners unintentionally: the Go 1.24 GODEBUG default is multipathtcp=2 (enabled). The Go Security Team recommends a patched kernel over disabling MPTCP per-program; the IPv4 lifetime bug persists even with MPTCP off, so only the kernel fix is durable. The ordinary IPv6 child path is unaffected because it duplicates options, though a separate IPv6 CALIPSO request-migration concern is handled elsewhere.
summary: CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP handshake path, where tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() hands the request socket's ireq_opt pointer to the child socket without duplicating it while a retransmitted SYN on another CPU still reads the same IP options object under RCU; destructors freed it with plain kfree() instead of kfree_rcu(), so memory could be reused mid-read. The upstream fix (commit e3f33b0a1d89) aligns reclamation with the readers' synchronization model by deferring frees to an RCU grace period, and also covers a request-migration variant that appears with net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 or reuseport BPF migration. The Linux CNA scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 while Ubuntu publishes a CVSS 4.0 8.3; the article argues these, plus a research exploit, answer different questions and none measures real-world prevalence. Anthropic reported a zero-click PoC that achieved unauthenticated root execution against an MPTCP listener in a controlled lab, leaking a kernel pointer in about 48 minutes and reaching command execution in about 5 more, with cheap retries after failed attempts. The piece flags that Go 1.24 enables MPTCP by default (GODEBUG multipathtcp=2), so Go servers may be exposed unintentionally, and that disabling MPTCP does not remove the underlying IPv4 bug. It stresses that upstream version strings cannot label vendor kernels because of backports, and recommends confirming the fix via vendor advisories, changelogs, or VEX statements, patching MPTCP-exposed and internet-facing hosts first, and rebooting Kubernetes nodes since containers share the host kernel.
novelty: RCU vs kfree lifetime mismatch in TCP request socket IP options
audience: kernel/security engineers managing Linux TCP-exposed infrastructure

title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
why: If you are bolting a dedicated memory layer onto a long-horizon agent, this paper argues your baseline should be plain RAG over raw history, because across its benchmarks the memory system often scored worse.
notes: The claim: in a self-described large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, many dedicated memory systems underperformed naive RAG in many cases, which the authors read as negative net value. No specific numbers, system names, or benchmark names appear in the abstract text provided.

The framework uses RAG as the reference point and splits a memory system's net value into 'memory benefit' (gains over direct retrieval) and 'memory tax' (losses). Both come from the same cause: memory processing reorganizes and distills raw history.
Mechanism of the tax: operations meant to help, such as reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, can also remove or obscure evidence that was present in the raw history, degrading retrieval.

The paper's stated contribution is conceptual framing plus measurement, arguing evaluations should shift from standalone memory performance to net value relative to retrieval; it generalizes 'memory tax' to further memory application scenarios.

Authors say they will open-source code and results via a project page. The arXiv identifier (2610.34073) and the abstract alone do not disclose methodology details, so the comparison setup and statistical basis cannot be verified from this text.
summary: The paper argues that the net value of building agent memory, versus directly retrieving from raw interaction history, is unclear and sometimes negative. Across what the authors describe as a large-scale evaluation spanning multiple benchmarks and model backbones, many dedicated memory systems underperformed naive RAG. Using RAG as a reference baseline, the authors decompose a memory system's effect into 'memory benefit' (gains from reorganizing facts or distilling preferences) and 'memory tax' (losses when that same processing removes or obscures evidence that existed in raw history). They treat these as two sides of the deviation memory introduces away from the raw record and focus attention on the under-studied tax, examining how it arises from both system design and evaluation choices and extending the concept to more scenarios. The stated goal is to move evaluation from standalone memory performance toward net value relative to retrieval. Code and results are promised as open source; the provided abstract gives no specific numbers, system names, or methodology.
novelty: quantifies when agent memory systems underperform plain RAG
audience: engineers building long-horizon LLM agents with memory modules

title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
why: If you continually pretrain or fine-tune an untied gated/hybrid checkpoint (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a single near-zero embedding row can silently zero out ~20% of your gradient updates while standard FP32 clipping in PyTorch, HF Trainer, and FSDP2 overflows to infinity.
notes: Census of 291 open-weight repos (280 distinct embedding tables): 52.6% of untied gated/hybrid checkpoints (20/38) have reachable input embeddings with norm below 1e-6, versus 0% of weight-tied models. The authors attribute near-zero rows to unseen rare/template tokens getting zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings.

Mechanism: at zero input, SiLU gates or linear queries vanish, suppressing historical-state readout; residual RMS can drop below the RMSNorm floor so Pre-RMSNorm amplifies backward gradients by up to 1e3 per layer. Reported input-embedding gradient amplification reaches up to 35 orders of magnitude in gated models.

Failure trigger: when a gradient entry exceeds 1.84e19, FP32 global-norm clipping overflows to infinity and zeros the whole batch's gradients. Transformers avoid this when a BOS token or non-initial position is present, per the tested configs.
Case study (self-reported): Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B discarded updates on roughly 20% of steps and left triggered embedding rows frozen.

Two fixes: GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm, claimed to eliminate update loss and heal triggered rows in one step with negligible measured overhead; GateFloor (SiLU(z)+delta, delta in [0.01,0.1]) keeps the gate positive at zero input, cutting near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude with perplexity comparable to baseline.

Scope caveat: GateFloor and scaling experiments run up to 370M parameters; the 4B result is a single continual-pretraining case, and all numbers are from the authors' own runs with released code (embscan/, mitigations/, verify_reproducibility.py).
summary: The paper documents a silent training-stall bug in untied gated and hybrid sequence models. A survey of 291 open-weight repositories (280 distinct embedding tables) finds that 52.6% of untied gated/hybrid checkpoints (20 of 38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below 1e-6, compared with 0% of weight-tied models; the authors attribute these to rare or template tokens receiving zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, and xLSTM, a near-zero token makes SiLU gates or linear queries vanish, and Pre-RMSNorm then amplifies backward gradients by up to 1e3 per layer, yielding gradient amplification up to 35 orders of magnitude. When an entry exceeds 1.84e19, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 overflows to infinity and zeros the batch; in Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B this discarded about 20% of steps and froze affected rows. The authors propose GroupClip (64-bit or rescaled embedding-norm clipping) to heal released checkpoints and GateFloor (SiLU(z)+delta) during pretraining, reporting a 28-order-of-magnitude reduction in near-zero gradients with comparable perplexity in experiments up to 370M parameters. Results are self-reported with released reproduction code.
novelty: silent training-stalling bug found in 52.6% of surveyed gated/hybrid LM checkpoints
audience: researchers/engineers pretraining or fine-tuning Mamba/xLSTM/hybrid gated sequence models

title: I Toured Unitree's Factory. I'm More Bullish on the West
why: The economics here say the money in humanoids is in building the motor lines, not the robots: at Unitree labor is 8% of cost, so the Western play is machines that make actuators, not hand-assembly plants in Ohio.
notes: Unitree's books: ~$1.7M total machinery against ~32,000 robots made in 2025, roughly $50 of machinery per robot; labor was 8% of production cost, so halving it saves ~4%. The new motor line is expected to cut per-motor labor by more than half and one robot model's cost by under 2% (about 9% at American wages).

A viral Unitree video (28M views) shows a humanoid doing assembly and calls it 'an actual deployment,' but the IPO prospectus calls it a pilot and says assembly is 'currently mainly manual.' The author saw humans on old winding machines, not robot lines.

Unitree's own slide puts robots' 'ChatGPT moment' (80% success on 80% of unseen tasks) two to three years out. Three quarters of humanoid revenue in the first nine months of 2025 came from research/education, under 5% from industrial work, and the author claims half or more of filed 'industry' revenue is robots giving guided tours.

Policy drivers: in July the FCC stopped approving new humanoids/robot dogs unless made in America with >65% US parts by cost (75% from 2029); Pentagon drone programs require stators wound outside China from August 2027. On Oct 28 the White House found the US 'relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics, industrial machinery.'

Western volume claims (all self-reported): Figure says BotQ went from one humanoid a day to one an hour in under four months; Tesla says most of a million-Optimus-a-year line is at Fremont; Agility listed on Nasdaq Nov 5 with Foxconn leading ~$201M despite selling just $1.8M of robots last year; 1X says it builds actuators from copper spool to finished part on self-designed lines in Hayward.

Caveat the author concedes: China passed Germany as top machine-tool exporter last year, all top-ten solar-equipment makers were Chinese by 2022, and Chinese hairpin-winding-line builders have undercut German/Italian rivals by up to half and export whole lines to Europe. The author discloses investments in several Western manufacturing/humanoid startups (Standard Manufacturing, Dirac, Isembard, RMFG, Minerva).
summary: Josef Chen, founder of KAIKAKU, reports from a tour of Unitree's Hangzhou factory that the plant is mostly manual: humans run winding machines, total machinery is worth about $1.7M against ~32,000 robots made in 2025, and labor is only 8% of production cost. He argues this is rational because Unitree ships a new robot design every year, so custom automation for a fast-changing product becomes scrap, and because humanoids are still mostly research tools (three quarters of humanoid revenue is research/education, under 5% industrial). Unitree is automating joint/motor modules first because the motor is the most standardized, least-changing part. Chen's thesis is that automation only pays once a product freezes, and that the real opportunity is building the machines and motor lines rather than robots, especially in the West where labor costs roughly six times more (making labor ~40% of cost) and US policy (FCC content rules, Pentagon stator requirements) shuts out Chinese hands. He cites historical analogues (Ford's Highland Park, GM's 1927 flexibility edge over a frozen Model T, Foxconn's unmet million-robot pledge) and self-reported Western progress from Figure, Tesla, Agility, and 1X, while conceding China now leads in machine tools and motor-line equipment. A promised part 2 covers his BYD visit, where he says everything he saw was automated with off-the-shelf Fanuc and KUKA arms.
novelty: firsthand data showing Unitree's factory is mostly manual, not robot-run
audience: readers tracking robotics/humanoid manufacturing and China-vs-West automation race

title: AlpineBSD
why: If you want a Unix base you can audit without wondering which lines came from an LLM, here is a distribution that bans AI-generated code from its kernel, libc, and main package repo as a design constraint.
notes: Stack: NetBSD kernel, libc, and platform tools like mount, paired with an Alpine Linux-inspired userspace using apk-tools and busybox, with a GNU lean (GNU make over BSD make).
Stated AI policy: no LLM output in the base system or main package repository; the project frames minimizing AI-generated software as its central objective.
Init: uses s6 now, not Alpine's OpenRC; adding OpenRC as an alternative is a stated plan, not shipped.
Not a fork of Alpine Linux; the package collection is described as original though many packages are ultimately based on aports.
Maturity caveat: no installer yet, only a high-level manual install guide; the site calls it a work in progress.
Hardware caveat inherited from NetBSD: the kernel has spotty hardware support, much weaker than Linux, especially for laptops; consult the NetBSD supported hardware list.
summary: AlpineBSD is an early-stage operating system built on the NetBSD kernel and libc with a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux, using apk-tools and busybox and a slightly more GNU-oriented toolchain. Its stated objective is to use as little AI-generated software as possible; the project claims no LLM output is included in the base system or main package repository. It currently uses the s6 init system rather than Alpine's OpenRC, with plans to add OpenRC as an alternative. The package collection is described as original rather than a fork of Alpine's aports, though many packages are ultimately based on them. The project is a work in progress with no installer yet, only a high-level manual installation guide. It inherits NetBSD's limited hardware support, which the site warns is much weaker than Linux, particularly for laptops.
novelty: NetBSD-based OS explicitly banning AI-generated code
audience: systems/OS engineers and devs skeptical of AI-generated code quality

title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
why: Running a coding agent against your real checkout means one prompt injection can touch your working tree and .git hooks; this gives each project a per-folder VM where the agent sees placeholders instead of your Claude or Codex tokens and reaches only an allowlisted set of hosts by default.
notes: Four network tiers per VM: allowlist (default), internet, open, none. The allowlist routes through a proxy on the host that swaps placeholder values in the VM for real secrets (Claude Code token, Codex login) only on outbound requests, so the VM never holds them.

Built on Lima: Apple's Virtualization framework on macOS, QEMU on Linux; arm64 or x86_64. First VM builds a base image; later VMs are copies that start in seconds, and each toolchain version is built once and shared read-only.

The VM mounts the project folder at the same path and sees nothing else in your home directory except agent settings, mounted read-only; agents get your settings, skills, and MCP servers but not your history.

--clone works on a separate repo clone so the agent can't touch your working tree or .git until you fetch; on macOS, devvm locks .git hooks and config so the VM can't change what git runs on the host.

.git protection is absent on Linux (listed under known limits). The project itself states no sandbox closes every gap and ships 'attack vectors' and 'staying safe' pages. Runs Claude Code, Codex, and opencode; supports devcontainer.json and --from (e.g. node:24).
Open source under MIT, installed via Homebrew (which also pulls Lima); on Linux, Lima additionally needs QEMU and /dev/kvm access. Self-describing claims; no independent security audit cited.
summary: devvm is an MIT-licensed, Homebrew-installed CLI that gives each project folder an isolated VM preloaded with the project's toolchain and a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, or opencode), aimed at limiting the blast radius of prompt injections, rogue agents, and leaked secrets. It runs on macOS and Linux via Lima (Apple Virtualization on macOS, QEMU on Linux), building a base image once and cloning fast-starting copies that share toolchains read-only. The VM mounts only the project folder plus read-only agent settings, and by default uses an allowlist network tier whose host-side proxy injects real agent secrets into outbound requests so the VM holds only placeholders; looser (internet, open) and stricter (none) tiers are available. It supports devcontainer.json, --from to base on any container image, custom layers, --clone to isolate the working tree and .git, and automatic port forwarding plus VS Code Remote-SSH. The project is explicit that no sandbox is complete and documents remaining attack vectors; notable gaps include .git hook/config protection being macOS-only. All security properties are the project's own claims with no cited external audit.
novelty: per-project disposable VM sandboxes tailored for coding agents
audience: developers running Claude Code/Codex/opencode agents who want sandbox isolation without config

title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, agents can drop 70-89% of tool-output tokens and 24-56% of runtime by feeding observations as latent embeddings instead of text, cutting the per-step cost that dominates multi-step web-search loops.
notes: Coca-Cola compresses raw tool outputs into continuous latent tokens and injects them directly into the agent's input embedding space, bypassing discrete text; the authors argue token pruning and summarization are capped by their reliance on text representations.

Action-Preserving Training aligns the agent's next-action distribution under full vs. compressed observations, so the compressor is optimized to keep decision-critical signal rather than reconstructing readable text.
Reported results: 70.01%-89.24% reduction in agent token consumption and 24.45%-55.97% reduction in end-to-end runtime, with task performance said to improve consistently.
Evaluation is limited to web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families; benchmark names, model identities, and baseline methods are not given in the abstract.
All figures are self-reported by the authors with no external replication; code is released, but the abstract omits methodology detail needed to verify the gains.
summary: The paper proposes Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents that compresses tool observations into latent tokens embedded in the agent's input embedding space, rather than appending raw text outputs. It introduces Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distribution under full and compressed observations to retain decision-critical information. On web-search agents across four QA benchmarks and two model families, the authors report cutting token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97% while consistently improving task performance. The motivation is that long, noisy tool outputs inflate context and dilute attention, and that existing text-based pruning and summarization are limited by discrete representations. Code is released. The numbers are self-reported, and the abstract does not name the specific benchmarks, models, or baselines.
novelty: compresses tool outputs into latent embedding tokens, not text
audience: engineers building long-horizon LLM agents with heavy tool/context overhead

title: ChatGPT silently passes data between connectors and the bounty wants an ID card
why: If you ship an MCP server or ChatGPT connector, the trust boundary is the OAuth client, not the server URL: ChatGPT can route a confirmed follow-up call to a different connector and carry a one-time code across apps without telling the user.
notes: Repro setup: one ChatGPT account, two connectors pointing to the same MCP server. Connector A is a custom developer-mode connector; connector B is the published app-directory version. Each has its own OAuth client, so the server sees two separate clients for the same user.

The flow: the model calls a confirmation tool through connector A, its MCP Apps widget shows the change, the user confirms, and the widget sends a one-time confirmation code to the conversation via ui/message.
The bug: the model makes the follow-up call carrying that code silently through connector B instead of connector A, with no notice to the user.

It failed here only because the server bound the code to connector A's OAuth client and rejected redemption via connector B; every attempt in that conversation failed. This is a reporter claim from logged attempts, not a demonstrated data exfiltration.

The author argues a third-party connector sharing the same server URL would see the same silent switch leak one app's data to another provider absent server-side binding, since a shared URL can front separate tenants, partners, or environments.
Proposed fix: match tool calls to a connector by its OAuth client identity, and keep a follow-up call on the same connector and OAuth client that started the flow.
summary: A reporter on the OpenAI developer forum describes ChatGPT silently routing a follow-up tool call through a different connector than the one that started a flow. With two connectors enabled that point to the same MCP server but hold separate OAuth clients, the model called a confirmation tool through connector A; the user confirmed in connector A's widget, which emitted a one-time code via ui/message. ChatGPT then made the follow-up call carrying that code through connector B, with no user notification. The server rejected it because the code was bound to connector A's OAuth client, so no exploitation occurred in this case, but the author warns that a third-party connector sharing the same server URL could receive another app's data absent such binding. The argument is that two connectors sharing an MCP URL are not one app, because the same URL can represent different tenants or parties per OAuth client. The requested fix is to scope tool calls to the originating connector's OAuth client rather than the server URL. Surfaced on Hacker News (83 points, 35 comments); the report is self-reported and not confirmed fixed by OpenAI in the text.
novelty: ChatGPT silently cross-routes tool calls between connectors sharing an MCP URL
audience: engineers building or securing MCP connectors/agent tooling

title: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’
why: A privacy vendor's leadership told employees to stop pentesting before shipping and to justify AI usage or risk firing, which bears directly on whether Proton's security products can be trusted.
notes: Andy Yen cancelled near company-wide 're-interviews' that would have forced employees to explain their AI usage, with the implication that insufficient use could lead to firing, according to six current employees and audio of a roughly two-hour all-hands obtained by 404 Media.

The cancellation followed a 404 Media investigation based on eight current and one former employee, Slack chats, meeting audio, and a CTO 'AI manifesto'; it came only after the story went public despite internal concerns.

In the security Slack channel in late August, Yen responded to a request to spend a few days pentesting new code before shipping by calling it 'bullshit and loser thinking' and told staff to 'stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.'

CTO Bart Butler's AI manifesto told engineers 'your old job is gone' and framed non-adoption as an 'existential threat to the success of the mission'; in the meeting Butler said 'we fucked up' and that Yen committed to communicating better.

Yen said he would 'still going to push,' that AI-usage metrics measured in re-interviews would become part of performance reviews, and that a reorganization proceeds next month, though 'there will be no loss of jobs from AI.'

Proton is owned by the Proton Foundation, whose board includes Yen, Tim Berners-Lee, Carissa Veliz, Dingchao Lu, and Antonio Gambardella; one employee noted Yen holds majority shares, limiting accountability. Users downvoted Yen's Reddit reply 1,200+ times, called for his resignation, and reported cancelling paid plans. Proton did not respond to a request for comment.
summary: 404 Media reports that Proton CEO Andy Yen cancelled a series of near company-wide 're-interviews' that would have required employees to explain their AI usage, with the implied threat of firing, a day after the outlet published an investigation into Proton's aggressive internal AI push. The reporting, based on nine current and former employees, Slack logs, all-hands audio, and CTO Bart Butler's 'AI manifesto,' describes Yen dismissing a request to pentest new code as 'bullshit and loser thinking' and telling staff to 'stop lovingly handcrafting all our code.' Butler's manifesto told engineers 'your old job is gone' and called non-adoption an existential threat to the mission. In the all-hands, Yen acknowledged a 'communication failure' and cancelled the re-interviews but said he would keep pushing AI, with usage metrics folded into performance reviews and a reorganization proceeding next month. Employees were split on whether this was genuine change or damage control, with some noting Yen's majority shareholding limits accountability. Proton users publicly called for Yen's resignation and reported cancelling paid plans over the apparent deprioritization of security; Proton did not respond to a request for comment.
novelty: CEO backtracks on forced AI adoption after internal leak
audience: engineers and security-conscious users following AI mandate backlash at tech companies

title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
why: The headline result: across seven LLM agents, closed-book "rediscovery" of math solved at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, and live-web gains mostly came from retrieving the published answer, so the benchmark gives a way to separate real reasoning from search.
notes: Two linked artifacts: a corpus of 12,151 open research problems across disciplines (recording statement, context, and progress), and a retrospective math benchmark of 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open.
Each benchmark problem carries a Lean 4 statement checked by automated probes plus two independent human reviews; HQ-50 is a quality-score-filtered subset.
Grading uses two independent proof checkers in an isolated sandbox under three conditions: closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web.
Closed-book rediscovery was rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems across seven agents under a standardized budget; live-web success largely tracked retrieving already-published solutions.

The design probes contamination directly by contrasting the three retrieval conditions, but the evaluation is limited to math and the public dataset/benchmark link is referenced rather than detailed in the abstract.
summary: OpenFrontiers pairs a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems with a retrospective math benchmark of 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each formalized as a Lean 4 statement verified by automated probes and two independent reviews. A quality-filtered HQ-50 subset is graded by two independent proof checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions, so the protocol can distinguish genuine rediscovery from retrieval of known answers. Evaluating seven LLM agents under a standardized budget, the authors report that closed-book rediscovery succeeded on at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, while live-web success mostly reflected finding published solutions. The stated goal is a formally graded foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and tracking progress on still-open scientific problems. The benchmark is confined to mathematics, and the reported figures are the authors' own.
novelty: benchmark distinguishing genuine rediscovery from web-search retrieval of known solutions
audience: AI researchers evaluating LLM scientific/mathematical reasoning capabilities

title: OpenIDEA: The IDE you know, rebuilt in Rust
why: If the numbers hold on your own projects, you get an IntelliJ-style editing environment that opens a ~770-file Python project in 1.1s on 169MB instead of 13.2s on 2GB, with the project's own perf/compare harness provided to check it.
notes: Native app with a Rust core, aiming to replicate IntelliJ IDEA's keymap, tool windows, and search-everything workflow; ships editor, code insight, debugger, Git, terminal, and database and HTTP clients for 60+ languages, with builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Self-reported benchmark (warm caches, median of 5 runs, freqtrade ~770 Python files): window-with-project 0.9s vs 3.1s, ready/CPU-settled 1.1s vs 13.2s, USS memory across all processes 169MB vs 2011MB, CPU time until ready 2.4s vs 47.9s, quit 0.3s vs 5.9s against IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3.
Test rig: release build of OpenIDEA from main, IDEA with default settings and plugins, on Windows 11, 32-core AMD, 62GB RAM; measured externally and reproducible via the perf/compare harness.
Stated caveat: 'ready' is not equivalent work on both sides because IDEA analyzes Python more deeply, so the readiness gap overstates comparable load.
Licensed Apache 2.0, not affiliated with JetBrains; IntelliJ IDEA is a JetBrains trademark. Idle CPU was close (4% vs 7% of a core), and the numbers are vendor-authored, not independently verified.
Surfaced on Hacker News at 28 points / 35 comments; deterministic relevance score 5.6/10.
