summary: OpenIDEA is an open-source (Apache 2.0) code editor built on a Rust core that copies IntelliJ IDEA's keymap, tool windows, and search-everything model, and bundles an editor, code insight, debugger, Git, terminal, and database and HTTP clients for 60+ languages, with builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The project is not affiliated with JetBrains. Its headline claim is a self-reported benchmark opening the freqtrade Python project (~770 files, warm caches, median of 5 runs on Windows 11, 32-core AMD, 62GB RAM): 1.1s to ready and 169MB USS versus 13.2s and 2011MB for IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3, with similarly large gaps in CPU time and quit time. The authors note the comparison is not strictly apples-to-apples because IDEA performs deeper Python analysis, so 'ready' does not represent identical work, and they publish a perf/compare harness to reproduce the measurements. The numbers are vendor-authored and not independently verified. It surfaced on Hacker News at 28 points and 35 comments.
novelty: Rust-based IntelliJ-keymap IDE claims 10x faster startup, 12x less memory
audience: JVM/polyglot devs wanting IntelliJ UX without JVM overhead

title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
why: Report URI can detect compromised sites faster than anyone can notify them, so 15,579 sites serving skimmers and malware to a claimed 135M monthly visits stay live for want of a working disclosure channel, not want of evidence.
notes: Report URI's threat-intel crawling has 15,579 unique sites confirmed infected with malicious JavaScript, plus thousands more at under-100% confidence; sites are dropped from the count once they self-clean, so the true total was higher.

The 135 million visits/month figure is the author's self-described ultra-conservative estimate; the sites skew to regional leaders (.fr, .es, .de) that rank high nationally but barely enter the global Top 1 Million.

Observed attack payloads: Magecart card skimmers on payment pages, ClickFix fake 'prove you're human' prompts that install malware, iOS exploit kits named DarkSword and Coruna, and redirects to phishing/scam pages.

Four infection vectors grouped: direct CMS compromise (e.g. WordPress), supply-chain script infection, classic XSS injection, and 'DeadTag', a group the author named that buys expired domains still referenced by live site JS and serves malware from them.
The bottleneck is disclosure, not detection: no contact info for crawled sites, low security.txt adoption, and mostly unanswered outreach make one-by-one notification unscalable.
The post is an open appeal: European NCSC/CERT teams are asked to email intel@report-uri.com for regional infected-site lists; the same address is offered for commercial threat-feed access.
summary: Scott Helme reports that Report URI's threat-intelligence crawling has identified 15,579 websites currently running malicious JavaScript, together receiving a self-described conservative estimate of over 135 million visits per month. Payloads seen include Magecart payment-page card skimmers, ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA malware installers, iOS exploit kits (DarkSword, Coruna), and malicious redirects, delivered via direct CMS/WordPress compromise, supply-chain script infection, XSS, or a newly named group called DeadTag that revives expired domains still referenced by site JavaScript. The core problem is that detection now far outpaces responsible disclosure: the team has no contact data for sites it crawls, security.txt adoption is low, and most outreach goes unanswered, making manual notification unscalable. Infected sites skew toward regional leaders in France, Spain, and Germany that rank high nationally but low globally. Helme asks for help and invites European CERTs/NCSCs to request regional lists at intel@report-uri.com, with the same address offered for commercial feed access. No methodology for the traffic estimate or the detection pipeline is detailed in the post.
novelty: scale of undisclosed web malware outpacing disclosure capacity
audience: security researchers, CERTs, web devs maintaining third-party scripts

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
why: An 8B open-weight model (Qwen3 8B) reportedly matches or beats AlphaEvolve's frontier-LLM results on some math-discovery problems while reaching other frameworks' best scores in 3-8 minutes instead of 60.
notes: The bottleneck it targets: LLM-guided evolutionary search is slow because each agent decodes a long textual chain of thought every round, repeated many times to keep population diversity.

Mechanism: hundreds of low-cost agents per round reason in latent space without decoding to text, and communicate by passing KV caches rather than strings; each swarm attacks the problem from a different angle.

Crossover happens in latent space: a summarizer agent ingests the combined KV caches of all swarm members. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct ideas by measuring distances between agents' hidden-state vectors.
Claimed results: across 21 mathematical-discovery and scientific-computing problems, highest average score and a median of 3-8 minutes to reach the best scores competing frameworks hit in 60 minutes.

On several problems, SwarmEvolve running Qwen3 8B is claimed to improve on solutions AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Caveat: numbers are self-reported in an arXiv abstract with no methodology, baseline configs, or per-problem detail shown here.
summary: SwarmEvolve is an LLM-guided evolutionary search framework that replaces per-agent textual chain-of-thought with hundreds of low-cost agents that reason in latent space and share information by passing KV caches instead of decoding to text. Each swarm studies a problem from a different angle; a novelty filter preserves diversity by measuring distances between agents' hidden-state vectors, and crossover occurs when a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 mathematical-discovery and scientific-computing problems the authors report the highest average score and a median of only 3-8 minutes to reach best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. They further claim that SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on some solutions AlphaEvolve first found using frontier LLMs. The results are self-reported in the abstract without methodology or baseline details provided in the text.
novelty: agents communicate via shared KV caches in latent space, not text
audience: ML researchers working on LLM-guided evolutionary search / program synthesis

title: Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave

Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) went further, calling for a day-one pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence, then sparred publicly with Elon Musk.

Sanders demanded an immediate national pause on X; Rep. Yassamin Ansari (AZ) pushed for a day-one halt on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence and clashed publicly with Elon Musk. Gabe Vasquez (NM), dozens of local ballot measures restricting datacenters, and moratorium pledges from incoming governors in Texas and Georgia, with Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa vowing to halt new projects pending protections. Industry figures reacted with concern — Meta's Dina Powell McCormick told WSJ building would get 'harder,' and the article links a week's AI stock selloff to regulation fears — while White House NEC director Kevin Hassett argued existing projects would be largely unaffected. The piece reports statements and campaign pledges rather than enacted legislation.

title: Libghostty 1.0
why: Ghostty's terminal engine is now a standalone 1.0 library, so you can embed a maintained terminal emulator in your own app or tool instead of writing one or forking the full editor.
notes: Announced by Mitchell Hashimoto, creator of Ghostty and co-founder of HashiCorp; the post marks libghostty reaching a 1.0 version.
libghostty is the terminal library carved out of the Ghostty terminal app, positioned for reuse independent of the full GUI application.
Surfaced on Hacker News at 163 points with 18 comments as of first capture on 2026-11-06.

title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
why: Libdragon now ships a codec that gives N64 homebrew near-Opus audio quality for ~4% CPU, so recorded music and speech fit alongside gameplay instead of eating most of the cartridge: the Half-Life N64 port used it to pack 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks into one 64MB image.
notes: ULC (Ultra Low Complexity Codec) by Aikku93, worked on since 2019, originated as a Game Boy Advance demo playing recorded music at 70kbps on a 16MHz ARM CPU with no vector instructions; permissively licensed.

It is a transform codec like MP3: full-band MDCT (no subband split), but coefficients stored as 4-bit signed nibbles with reserved values for zero runs, long zero runs, quantizer changes, and noise fill, so there is no Huffman/entropy coding or arbitrary bit reads. Coefficient unpacking is ~150 lines of C.

Prior options were poor: Libultra/Libdragon ADPCM gives only 4x compression (a 5-min 44.1kHz stereo track is ~12MB versus 8-64MB cartridges), and Libdragon's RSP Opus decoder is high quality but too CPU-heavy for real-time gameplay.

Porting to the RSP required fitting an IMDCT into 4096 bytes of DMEM; the author moved from float to 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14), choosing a 1024-sample block with 512-sample lap buffer (3072 bytes) over the default 2048, trading a higher noise floor for less DMA and faster compute.

RSP port is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling, barely fitting the 4096-byte IMEM; written iteratively with Codex translating C to Max Bebök's RSPL language, with the author distrusting GPT-5 for direct RSP assembly.

Self-reported result: 44.1kHz stereo at near-Opus bitrate costs ~4% CPU and ~5% RSP time, complexity ~4x ADPCM; usable down to 16kbps; a sparse seek table (every eighth frame) adds ~20 bytes/sec. Merged into Libdragon's preview branch.
summary: The author (phoboslab) describes adapting ULC, the Ultra Low Complexity Codec created by Aikku93 for a Game Boy Advance demo, to run on the Nintendo 64's RSP coprocessor within Libdragon. ULC is a transform codec similar to MP3 but uses a full-band MDCT and stores coefficients in a nibble-based syntax (4-bit signed values with reserved codes for zero runs, quantizer changes, and noise fill) rather than Huffman entropy coding, making decoding simple and vectorizable. To fit the IMDCT into the RSP's 4KB DMEM, the author converted the float reference decoder to 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14) with a 1024-sample block, then ported it to ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly (via the RSPL language and Codex) that just fits the 4KB IMEM. The reported result is 44.1kHz stereo at near-Opus bitrates using about 4% CPU and 5% RSP time, roughly 4x the complexity of ADPCM, suitable for real-time background music and speech where Opus was too slow and ADPCM too space-hungry. The codec is merged into Libdragon's preview branch, and a recent Half-Life N64 port reportedly used it to fit 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks into a single 64MB cartridge. Performance and quality figures are the author's own, described qualitatively ("faintest white noise") rather than with formal measurements.
